poetic_form.description: The Castle of Nourishing is a ribald poetic form intended to praise fortresses, originating in The Standards of Driving. The form guides poets during improvised performances. The poem is a single couplet. A form of parallelism is common throughout the poem, in that certain lines reverse grammatical structures. The ending of each line of the poem shares the same rhyme. The second line of the couplet shares the underlying meaning of the first line. The second line of the couplet presents a different view of the subject of the first line. The second line of the couplet must expand the idea of the first line. The first line has six syllables. The second line has nine syllables.

The Laconic Quiescence is a ribald poetic form concerning a historical figure, originating in The Standards of Driving. The rules of the form are applied by poets to produce individual poems which can be recited. The poem is divided into three distinct parts: a series of sexains, a series of quintains and another series of sexains. Use of allegory and symbolism is characteristic of the form. [B]The first part is intended to describe the subject of the poem. The fifth line of each sexain is required to maintain the phrasing of the second line. It has lines with nine syllables. The rhyme scheme respecting the full poem is AABACA. [B]The second part is intended to develop the previous idea. Certain lines are required to maintain phrasing. It has lines with nine syllables. The rhyme scheme respecting the full poem is ABAAB. [B]The third part is intended to renounce. Certain lines are required to maintain phrasing. It has lines with four syllables. The rhyme scheme respecting the full poem is DDEDEE.

The Scholarly Queen is a poetic form, originating in The Standards of Driving. The form guides poets during improvised performances. The poem is divided into three to four quatrains and two couplets. Use of assonance is characteristic of the form. Forms of parallelism are common throughout the poem, in that certain lines often share an underlying meaning and they use the same placement of allusions. Each line has nine syllables. [B]The first part is intended to describe the past. The rhyme scheme respecting the full poem is ABAA. [B]The second part is intended to reflect on previous ideas concerning the future. The rhyme scheme respecting the full poem is BB.

The Canyons of Cobalt is a dramatic poetic form concerning mining, originating in The Standards of Driving. The form guides poets during improvised performances. The poem is divided into numerous series of sexains and numerous series of ten-line stanzas. A form of parallelism is common throughout the poem, in that certain lines use the same placement of allusions. [B]The first part is intended to make an assertion. The sixth line of each sexain is required to maintain the phrasing of the fourth line. The sixth line of each sexain must expand the idea of the fourth line. It has lines with seven syllables. It has a terminal caesura in each line. The rhyme scheme respecting the full poem is AAABBB. [B]The second part is intended to invert the previous assertion. The ninth line of each stanza is required to maintain the phrasing of the second line. The sixth line of each stanza must expand the idea of the third line. It has lines with five syllables. It has a medial caesura in each line. The rhyme scheme respecting the full poem is CCCDCDDCDC.

The Poetic Desserts is a poetic riddle concerning someone recently retired, originating in The Standards of Driving. The rules of the form are applied by poets to produce individual poems which can be recited. The poem is divided into three distinct parts: two couplets, a line and two quatrains. Forms of parallelism are common throughout the poem, in that certain lines often contrast underlying meaning and they use the same placement of allusions. Every line of the poem has an initial caesura. [B]The first part is intended to describe the subject of the poem. Certain lines sometimes have reversed word orders. It has lines with nine syllables. The rhyme scheme respecting the full poem is AA. [B]The second part is intended to develop the previous idea. It has six syllables. [B]The third part is intended to teach a moral lesson. The fourth line of each quatrain reverses the word order of the second line. It has lines with five syllables. The rhyme scheme respecting the full poem is AAAA.

The Lessons of Quiescence is a dramatic poetic form, originating in The Standards of Driving. The rules of the form are applied by poets to produce individual poems which can be recited. The poem is a single couplet. Use of juxtaposition is characteristic of the form. Every line of the poem has an initial caesura. The ending of each line of the poem shares the same rhyme. The second line of the couplet has the same grammatical structure as the first line. The first line is intended to describe the past. It has eleven syllables. The second line is intended to offer a different perspective concerning the future. It must make use of consonance. It has eight syllables.

The Adorable Festival is a reflective poetic form intended to satirize a specific wilderness region, originating in The Mischievous Shores. The rules of the form are applied by poets to produce individual poems which can be recited. The poem is a single quatrain. Use of assonance and ambiguity is characteristic of the form. A form of parallelism is common throughout the poem, in that certain lines sometimes have reversed word orders. Each line has five feet with a tone pattern of uneven-even-uneven. The second line of the quatrain contrasts the underlying meaning of the first line.

The Blossom of Heather is a poetic form intended to express pleasure with the concept of nature, originating in The Mischievous Shores. The rules of the form are applied by poets to produce individual poems which can be recited. The poem is a single couplet. A form of parallelism is common throughout the poem, in that certain lines often contrast underlying meaning. Every line of the poem has a medial caesura. The first line has eight feet with a tone pattern of uneven-even-even. The second line has eight feet with a tone pattern of even-uneven.

The Mind of Berries is a poetic form intended to express grief over a chosen subject, originating in The Mischievous Shores. The rules of the form are applied by poets to produce individual poems which can be recited. The poem is a single tercet. Use of antanaclasis is characteristic of the form. Forms of parallelism are common throughout the poem, in that certain lines often contrast underlying meaning, they are required to maintain phrasing, they have similar grammatical structures and they reverse grammatical structures. Every line of the poem has a terminal caesura. The first line concerns the past. It has three feet with a tone pattern of even-uneven-even. The second line concerns current events. It has three feet with a tone pattern of even-uneven-even. The third line concerns the future. It has five feet with a tone pattern of even-uneven-even.

musical_form.description: The Puce Jewels is a devotional form of music directed toward the worship of Rakas originating in The Standards of Driving. The form guides musicians during improvised performances. One to two singers recite The Canyons of Cobalt while the music is played on a mokez. The musical voices bring melody and counterpoint. The entire performance should be lively and is moderately paced. The melody has mid-length phrases, while the counterpoint has phrases of varied length throughout the form. It is performed in free rhythm. Throughout, when possible, performers are to modulate frequently and play legato. [B]Each singer always is to be moderately loud. [B]The mokez always is to be loud. [B]The Puce Jewels has a well-defined multi-passage structure: a lengthy introduction and a theme and a series of variations on the theme. [B]The introduction is voiced by the melody of the singers and the counterpoint of the mokez. Each of the singers' voices stays in the low register and the mokez stays in the liquid high register. Only one pitch is ever played at a time in this passage. The passage is performed using the kulet scale. [B]The theme is voiced by the melody of the mokez and the counterpoint of the singers. The mokez covers its entire range and each of the singers' voices ranges from the middle register to the high register. This passage features only melodic tones and intervals. The passage is performed using the bidok scale. The passage should be performed using melismatic phrasing. [B]The series of variations is voiced by the melody of the mokez and the counterpoint of the singers. The mokez covers its entire range and each of the singers' voices stays in the low register. Chords are packed close together in dense clusters in this passage. The passage is performed using the alak scale. [B]Scales are constructed from thirteen notes dividing the octave. In quartertones, their spacing is roughly 1-x-x-x--x-x-xx-x-x-xx-xO, where 1 is the tonic, O marks the octave and x marks other notes. The tonic note is a fixed tone passed from teacher to student. After a scale is constructed, notes are named according to degree. The names are mabdug (spoken ma), zustash (zu), sedil (se), ustos (us), em„r (em), izeg (iz) and bem•ng (be). [B]The kulet hexatonic scale is constructed by selection of degrees from the fundamental scale. The degrees selected are the 1st, the 3rd, the 6th, the 7th, the 9th and the 10th. [B]The bidok heptatonic scale is constructed by selection of degrees from the fundamental scale. The degrees selected are the 1st, the 3rd, the 6th, the 8th, the 9th, the 10th and the 12th. [B]The alak hexatonic scale is constructed by selection of degrees from the fundamental scale. The degrees selected are the 1st, the 4th, the 6th, the 8th, the 9th and the 11th.

The Mother of Rhyme is a form of music used during marches and military engagements originating in The Standards of Driving. The form guides musicians during improvised performances. The music is played on a dast. The entire performance should be melancholic and is at a free tempo. The melody has mid-length phrases throughout the form. It is performed using the anam scale and in the fer rhythm. Throughout, when possible, performers are to alternate tension and repose and play arpeggios. [B]The dast always does the main melody. [B]The Mother of Rhyme has a well-defined multi-passage structure: an introduction, a chorus and a lengthy verse, a bridge-passage and a chorus and a verse. [B]The introduction is to be moderately loud. The dast ranges from the resonant low register to the dull middle register. This passage features only melodic tones and intervals. [B]The first chorus is to be in whispered undertones. The dast stays in the resonant low register. Only one pitch is ever played at a time in this passage. [B]The first verse is to be very soft. The dast ranges from the dull middle register to the heavy high register. Chords are packed close together in dense clusters in this passage. The passage should be performed using mordents. [B]The bridge-passage is to be moderately loud. The dast stays in the resonant low register. This passage typically has some sparse chords. The passage should be performed using mordents. [B]The second chorus is to be loud. The dast covers its entire range from the resonant low register to the heavy high register. Chords are packed close together in dense clusters in this passage. The passage should be performed using mordents. [B]The second verse is to be very loud. The dast stays in the dull middle register. Chords are packed close together in dense clusters in this passage. The passage should be performed using mordents. [B]Scales are constructed from thirteen notes dividing the octave. In quartertones, their spacing is roughly 1-x-x-x--x-x-xx-x-x-xx-xO, where 1 is the tonic, O marks the octave and x marks other notes. The tonic note is a fixed tone passed from teacher to student. After a scale is constructed, notes are named according to degree. The names are mabdug (spoken ma), zustash (zu), sedil (se), ustos (us), em„r (em), izeg (iz) and bem•ng (be). [B]The anam hexatonic scale is constructed by selection of degrees from the fundamental scale. The degrees selected are the 1st, the 2nd, the 5th, the 7th, the 8th and the 10th. [B]The fer rhythm is a single line with sixteen beats divided into two bars in a 8-8 pattern. The beats are named uvel (spoken uv), dolush (do), agˆk (ag), ucat (uc), ng rak (ng ), enir (en), ugath (ug) and lisig (li). The beat is stressed as follows:[B]| x - - x x X - - | - - - x - - - - | [B]where X marks an accented beat, x is a beat, - is silent and | indicates a bar.

The Style of Embraces is a form of music used to commemorate important events originating in The Standards of Driving. The form guides musicians during improvised performances. A chanter recites nonsensical words and sounds while the music is played on two stibmer and a mokez. The musical voices bring melody, counterpoint and rhythm. The entire performance is moderately paced. The melody has long phrases, while the counterpoint has phrases of varied length throughout the form. It is performed using the gatal scale and in free rhythm. Throughout, when possible, performers are to alternate tension and repose. [B]The chanter always should be delicate. [B]Each stibmer always should sparkle and plays arpeggios. [B]The mokez always should be merry and plays arpeggios. [B]The Style of Embraces has a well-defined multi-passage structure: a first theme, an exposition of the first theme, a bridge-passage, a second theme, an exposition of the second theme, a lengthy bridge-passage, a synthesis of previous passages and a coda. [B]The first theme is voiced by the melody of the chanter reciting nonsensical words and sounds, the melody of the mokez and the counterpoint of the stibmer. The passage is to be moderately loud. The chanter's voice covers its entire range, the mokez covers its entire range and each of the stibmer ranges from the flat middle register to the sweet high register. Chords are packed close together in dense clusters in this passage. [B]The first exposition is voiced by the melody of the stibmer and the counterpoint of the chanter reciting nonsensical words and sounds. The passage is to be loud. Each of the stibmer ranges from the flat middle register to the sweet high register and the chanter's voice stays in the low register. This passage typically has some sparse chords. The passage should be performed using rapid runs. [B]The first bridge-passage is voiced by the melody of the mokez and the rhythm of the chanter reciting nonsensical words and sounds. The passage is to be moderately loud. The mokez covers its entire range and the chanter's voice covers its entire range. This passage is richly layered with full chords making use of the available range. [B]The second theme is voiced by the melody of the mokez, the counterpoint of the chanter reciting The Scholarly Queen and the counterpoint of the stibmer. The passage is to start loud then be immediately soft. The mokez covers its entire range, the chanter's voice stays in the high register and each of the stibmer covers its entire range from the buzzy low register to the sweet high register. Chords are packed close together in dense clusters in this passage. [B]The second exposition is voiced by the melody of the stibmer, the melody of the mokez and the rhythm of the chanter reciting The Scholarly Queen. The chanter's voice ranges from the low register to the middle register and the b„stza covers its entire range from the buzzy low register to the strident high register. Only one pitch is ever played at a time in this passage. [B]The second theme is at a free tempo. The chanter's voice ranges from the low register to the middle register and the b„stza stays in the buzzy low register. This passage typically has some sparse chords. The passage should be composed and performed using locally improvisation. The passage should always include a falling melody pattern with flattened third degree, sharpened fifth degree and flattened fourth degree as well as trills and arpeggios and sometimes include a rising-falling melody pattern with sharpened fourth degree on the fall. [B]The second exposition is slower than the last passage. The chanter's voice ranges from the middle register to the high register and the b„stza stays in the buzzy low register. Only one pitch is ever played at a time in this passage. [B]The synthesis is extremely fast. The chanter's voice ranges from the middle register to the high register and the b„stza stays in the buzzy low register. Only one pitch is ever played at a time in this passage. [B]Scales are conceived of as two chords built using a division of the perfect fourth interval into eleven notes. The tonic note is a fixed tone passed from teacher to student. The Scintillating Silkiness is a form of music used for entertainment originating in The Immorality of Play. The rules of the form are applied by composers to produce individual pieces of music which can be performed. The music is played on a urab. Only one pitch is ever played at a time. It is performed without preference for a scale and in the zud”l rhythm. Throughout, when possible, composers and performers are to syncopate. [B]The urab always provides the rhythm and should be passionate. [B]The Scintillating Silkiness has a well-defined multi-passage structure: a verse and a chorus all repeated one times and a brief finale. [B]The verse is slow, and it is to be moderately soft. [B]The chorus is moderately fast, and it is to become softer and softer. [B]The finale is half the tempo of the last passage, and it is to be very loud. [B]The rhythm system is fundamentally polyrhythmic. There are always multiple rhythm lines, and each of their bars is played over the same period of time, regardless of the number of beats. The rhythm lines are thought of as one, without a primary-subordinate relationship, though individual lines can be named. [B]The zud”l rhythm is a single line with two beats. The beats are named zaxo (spoken za) and ospo (os). The beat is stressed as follows:[B]| x'- | [B]where ' marks a beat as late, x is a beat, - is silent and | indicates a bar.

The Glosses of Playing is a form of music used during marches and military engagements originating in The Immorality of Play. The rules of the form are applied by composers to produce individual pieces of music which can be performed. A speaker recites a composition of The Pristine Sparkles while the music is played on three loma. The musical voices are joined in melody. The entire performance should bring a sense of motion and is at a free tempo, and it is to start loud then be immediately soft. The melody has mid-length phrases throughout the form. It is performed using the xenmu scale and in the smug rhythm. Throughout, when possible, composers and performers are to make trills and spread syllables over many notes. [B]In the finale, each of the loma stays in the fragile high register. This passage features only melodic tones and intervals. [B]Scales are conceived of as two chords built using a division of the perfect fourth interval into eleven notes. The tonic note is a fixed tone passed from teacher to student. There are always multiple rhythm lines, and each of their bars is played over the same period of time, regardless of the number of beats. The rhythm lines are thought of as one, without a primary-subordinate relationship, though individual lines can be named. [B]The smug rhythm is made from two patterns: the enu and the nolsmu. As stated above, they are to be played in polyrhythm. [B]The enu rhythm is a single line with eight beats. The beats are named st”l (spoken st”), zak (za), tuxxu (tu), ugas (ug), ustrok (us), gosma (go), k†bu (k†) and ron (ro). The beat is stressed as follows:[B]| X x - - x`| x`X x x x | - x - X x | x - x'X x | - - x - - | [B]where X marks an accented beat, ` marks a beat as early, ' marks a beat as late, x is a beat, - is silent and | indicates a bar.

[B]The nol rhythm is a single line with thirty-two beats divided into eight bars in a 4-4-4-4-4-4-4-4 pattern. The beat is stressed as follows:[B]| - - - x | - - x - | - - - x | - x x - | x - x - | x X x x`| - X x x | - - x - | [B]where X marks an accented beat, ` marks a beat as early, x is a beat, - is silent and | indicates a bar. The Verse of Rhymes is a form of music used during marches and military engagements originating in The Immorality of Play. The form guides musicians during improvised performances. The beat is stressed as follows:[B]| - - - x | - - x - | - - - x | - x x - | x - x - | x X x x`| - X x x | - - x - | [B]where X marks an accented beat, ` marks a beat as early, x is a beat, - is silent and | indicates a bar. The beat is stressed as follows:[B]| - - x'- x X - x`| [B]where X marks an accented beat, ` marks a beat as early, ' marks a beat as late, x is a beat, - is silent and | indicates a bar.

The Chartreuse Queen is a form of music used during marches and military engagements originating in The Sloppy Empires. The form guides musicians during improvised performances. The music is played on a anba. The entire performance should be delicate. The melody has long phrases throughout the form. Chords, seldom-used, are sparse -- intervals and single pitches are favored. It is performed using the ramet scale and in the arin rhythm. Throughout, when possible, performers are to use mordents and modulate frequently. [B]The anba always does the main melody and glides from note to note. The voice stays in the liquid high register. [B]The Chartreuse Queen has a simple structure: a passage. [B]The simple passage is moderately paced, and it is to be in whispered undertones. [B]Scales are conceived of as two chords built using a division of the perfect fourth interval into eleven notes. The beat is stressed as follows:[B]| - - x x | - - x - | - - x x | x - x - | [B]where x is a beat, - is silent and | indicates a bar.

The Droplet of Drumming is a form of music used for entertainment originating in The Sloppy Empires. The Rhyme of Smiling is a form of music used to commemorate important events originating in The Sloppy Empires. The form guides musicians during improvised performances. The music is played on a tusus. The entire performance is to be in whispered undertones. Only one pitch is ever played at a time. It is performed without preference for a scale and in free rhythm. [B]The tusus always provides the rhythm and should be passionate. [B]The Rhyme of Smiling has a simple structure: three brief unrelated passages. [B]Each of the simple passages is at a hurried pace. Each passage should be performed using legato.

The Phrase of Lilacs is a devotional form of music originating in The Sloppy Empires. The rules of the form are applied by composers to produce individual pieces of music which can be performed. The rhythm lines are thought of as one, without a primary-subordinate relationship, though individual lines can be named. The Natural Sun-Hides is a devotional form of music directed toward the worship of Inale the Sunken Scale originating in The Livid Lark. The form guides musicians during improvised performances. A chanter recites a composition of The Vale of Submerging while the music is played on a ˜emi, a ofa and three iyilo. The musical voices bring melody, counterpoint and rhythm. The entire performance is consistently slowing. The melody has short phrases, while the counterpoint has mid-length phrases throughout the form. Never more than an interval sounds at once. It is performed in free rhythm. Throughout, when possible, performers are to alternate tension and repose and spread syllables over many notes. [B]The chanter always does the counterpoint melody and should be stately. [B]The ˜emi always does the main melody and should bring a sense of motion. The voice ranges from the rich low register to the floating middle register. [B]The ofa always provides the rhythm and should perform with feeling. The ˜emi ranges from the rich low register to the floating middle register, the chanter's voice covers its entire range and the ofa covers its entire range from the raspy low register to the buzzy high register. Each passage is performed using the datha scale. [B]The coda is to be in whispered undertones. The ˜emi ranges from the rich low register to the floating middle register, the chanter's voice ranges from the middle register to the high register and the ofa stays in the watery middle register. In quartertones, their spacing is roughly 1-x-x-xx-xxx-xxxx-xx-x-xO, where 1 is the tonic, O marks the octave and x marks other notes. The tonic note is a fixed tone passed from teacher to student. [B]The datha pentatonic scale is constructed by selection of degrees from the fundamental scale. The degrees selected are the 1st, the 4th, the 8th, the 10th and the 13th.

dance_form.description: The Mauve Embraces is a solo performance dance originating in The Standards of Driving. The rules of the form are applied by choreographers to produce individual dances which can be performed. The dance is accompanied by a composition of The Poetic Pantomime of Smiles as the dancer acts out The Canyons of Cobalt. The dancer performs very slowly to the music's udir rhythm. This dance is a refined artform, with three special positions to be mastered. The entire dance has a basic movement called the bugsud. There is a series of three steps in a triangle pattern with a graceful raised right arm and a fluid sway. The dance is punctuated by relaxed arm carriage and crude counterclockwise quarter turns. [B]The dance begins with the theme of the music. This sluggish section is punctuated by relaxed facial expressions and high leg lifts. [B]The dance enters a new section with the variations on the theme of the music. This section is punctuated by low body level, grotesque left kicks and loudly percussive runs. [B]The okag is one of the fundamental dance positions. There should be a twisting backward bend. [B]The nazush is one of the fundamental dance positions. There should be an aggressive raised right arm with a vigorous leftward bend. [B]The nashon is one of the fundamental dance positions. There should be a debauched facial expression with a vivacious raised left arm and a relaxed leftward bend.

The Dye of Wanderers is a sacred group dance originating in The Standards of Driving. The form guides dancers during improvised performances. The dance is accompanied by The Puce Jewels. The dancers perform in a circle, moving with the music. This dance is a refined artform, with two special positions to be mastered. The spirited undulating dance is punctuated by proud footwork. [B]The dance enters a new section with the theme of the music. This vigorous section is punctuated by raised arms. [B]The ƒtrid is one of the fundamental dance positions. There should be a refined facial expression with a joyous raised arm. [B]The en“r is one of the fundamental dance positions. There should be a leg lift.

The Cardinal Intricacy is a war dance originating in The Standards of Driving. The form guides dancers during improvised performances. The dance is accompanied by The Chartreuse Sheens. The dancers perform in several lines turning counterclockwise, moving to the music's libash rhythm. The dance is punctuated by movement along the line of dance and leaps, with aborted moves. [B]The dance begins with the introduction of the music. The dancers perform very quickly with the music. This section is punctuated by rightward bends, raised left arms and expressive spins.
